name: Tracing the Data Behind a Tool
title: Tracing the Data Behind a Tool
answer: Tracing the data behind a tool means asking students to find out where an AI tool's data came from and to think about what that origin means. It matters because AI literacy includes evaluating and working with AI, and the text says coding is not a prerequisite. This idea gives teachers a way to build that literacy across grade bands while checking whether students actually learn it.

sections.body: This idea is an AI literacy unit in which students investigate a tool's data sources and interpret the consequences. The problem it solves is that students can use AI without understanding that machines learn from data, and the text notes that children under about 8 tend to overestimate how intelligent AI agents are. A framework of four aspects, knowing AI and understanding it, applying and using it, evaluating and creating with it, and thinking about its ethics, helps teachers organize the work. Younger students can focus on the first two aspects, while older students move toward evaluating tools and debating their use. Figure 8.6 in the text maps these aspects to grade bands.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In the classroom, teachers plan across grades using the four aspects of AI literacy. With younger students, the focus stays on knowing and understanding AI and on using and applying it, which fits the finding that even young children can be taught that machines learn from data. With older students, the work shifts toward evaluating tools and debating their use. The text says coding is not a prerequisite, so the unit does not depend on programming. Teachers can ask students to trace where a tool's data came from and what that means, and schools running such units should build in a simple before and after check.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text cites Long & Magerko, 2020, who reviewed 150 sources and defined AI literacy as competencies that let people evaluate AI, work with it, and use it well, and who found that coding is not a prerequisite. It also reports their note that children under about 8 tend to overestimate how intelligent AI agents are. Ng et al., 2021, proposed four aspects of AI literacy, and Figure 8.6 shows how those aspects map to grade bands. Casal-Otero et al., 2023, reviewed 179 documents on AI literacy in schools and found that few checked whether students actually learned what was taught. The text says much of this work has not yet been tested for learning results.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The main limit in the text is that much AI literacy work has not been tested for learning results, and a review of 179 documents found that few studies checked student learning. That means schools should not assume a unit works just because it is well designed. The text says schools running AI literacy units should build in a simple before and after check, which keeps the judgment local and evidence based. The risk for young children is that they may overestimate how intelligent AI agents are, so teaching must address how machines learn from data. The text leaves the planning choices, including which aspects to emphasize by grade band, with teachers and schools.
